## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)Abstract

### Purpose

The article is aimed at improving the understanding of the sociocultural profile of adult orthodontic patients and their expectations. In particular, it addresses three main aspects: the motivation and needs that underpin the decision to start orthodontic treatment, how it influences the patients' daily life, and the different oral hygiene demands.

### Materials and Methods

An online survey was completed by 276 patients undergoing orthodontic treatment with different techniques. The questions asked concerned gender, age, type of appliance, any previous orthodontic treatments, type of any previous retainers, reasons for therapy, satisfaction, pain, problems in eating, daily number of teeth brushings and flossings before and during the treatment, perception of cost, sensation of visibility of the appliance, and if they would recommend orthodontic treatment.

### Results

A significant role within our sample is played by gender; 87.94% consisted of female patients out of which 72.57% wanted to improve their aesthetics, while only 54.84% of male patients cited the same reason. Invisible aligners were preferred by 67.70% of the patients due to them being considered the least painful, causing the fewest problems with eating, and the least visible. Metal braces were perceived as the less expensive treatment. Over a third of the patients (33.85%) had previously undergone orthodontic treatment, among them 54.05% wore a mobile retainer, 31.08% a fixed one, and 14.86% both. Daily tooth brushing and flossing increased during therapy with clear aligners by 48.94% and 126.39%, respectively.

### Conclusions

The greatest demand for orthodontic treatments comes from women, as they pay more attention to aesthetics, which makes the clear aligners the most common choice. The relapse after orthodontic treatment seems to cause a higher demand for retreatment, and oral hygiene habits significantly improve during orthodontic treatment, especially with the clear aligners.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)1. Introduction

The demand for orthodontic treatments by adults, according to the surveys by the American Association of Orthodontists, is constantly increasing: in 2012, US orthodontists had an average of 129 adult patients; in 2014, it was 150; in 2016, it was 173; and in 2018, it was 178, with an overall increase of 27.53% in only six years. Likewise in 1960, the AAO survey reported that only 4.37% of the orthodontic patients were adults, while forty-six years later, according to the 2016 AAO survey, the adult patients were 28.31% of the total with the percentage rising as much as seven times higher.

A study by Muir et al. [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B1)] showed that in 1986, the adult orthodontic patients in New Zealand were 71% female. A similar study was published by Breece and Nieberg [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B2)] which reported that 76% of the adult orthodontic patients of their sample were female and over half were married. The study of Khan and Horrocks [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B3)] confirmed the data of 71% of female adult orthodontic patients. In 2011, Pabari et al. [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B4)] observed a percentage of 73% of females.

The interest of women vs. men in changing their dental look through orthodontic therapies is due to their higher aesthetic standards. Furthermore, a study published by Bolas-Colvee et al. [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B5)] in 2018 revealed that women are more critical of midline diastema, the “black triangle” (the space between gingiva and contact point of upper incisors, when present), and the gingival margin of the upper central incisor compared to men. So, their higher number of requests for treatment can be associated not only to a stronger desire of personal beauty but also to a more acute attention to the objective smile aesthetic details that impact their mouth.

The start of orthodontic therapy represents a novelty that can affect the patient's quality of life [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B6)]. This is related to the visibility of the appliance or braces in the mouth and the fact that improvements are achieved at a slower pace and also that the appliance or braces will be visible for a long time [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B7), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B8)].

Oral health influences the physical, social, and psychological well-being. It is undeniable that dental esthetics affect how people are perceived by society and how they perceive themselves [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B9)]. According to Isiekwe et al. [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B10)], there is a strict connection between oral health and quality of life in adults. This study highlights that poor dental esthetics can lead to feelings of shame and it negatively affects the person's image. So, it is clear that dental esthetics influence psychosocial aspects of life, and a good dental appearance can lead to a better social function.

Sun et al. [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B9)] reported that untreated malocclusions are connected to an increased negative impact on the health profile and psychosocial aspects.

Demirovic et al. [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B11)] compared adult patients who received an orthodontic treatment and the ones who did not. The results showed a remarkable negative impact of malocclusion on oral health related to quality of life (OHRQoL) in the ones who did not have therapy and a significant increase of the score on the oral health impact profile (OHIP) [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B12)].

Many adult patients ask for an orthodontic retreatment, due to an orthodontic relapse or unsatisfying previous treatments. Breece and Nieberg [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B2)] in 1986 reported that 6-7% of adult therapies are retreatments. This data was confirmed by Pabari et al. [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B4)] who reported that 12.6% of adult patients declared that they underwent a previous treatment which was not satisfactory.

The possibility to use less noticeable orthodontic solutions rather than the traditional vestibular metal braces persuaded many adult patients to begin orthodontic treatment. The clear aligners are currently the most popular mode, but adult patients appreciate the ceramic and the lingual braces as well. These kinds of appliances work better in adults, as they are more responsible and attentive to the doctor's recommendations in terms of the brackets' care and oral hygiene.

Another issue to be carefully considered in the orthodontic treatment of adults is their discomfort with the appliances. According to Afroz et al. [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B13)], pain can be caused by the presence of the appliances themselves, or by their chairside activation, including enamel interproximal reduction (IPR) procedures.

Proper oral hygiene maintenance during the orthodontic treatment is an important issue for both the clinician and the patients. The choice of esthetic appliances (clear aligners and lingual or ceramic brackets) should be guided by the patient's baseline clinical oral cavity condition which in adults might be worse than in teens. Aljohani and Alsaggaf [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B14)], a cross-sectional study including teen and adult patients, showed a significant improvement in the number of times and duration of daily teeth brushing and in the use of dental floss, so the patient's oral health-related behavior seems to improve during and after orthodontic treatment. In a prospective randomized clinical trial among teen patients, Chhibber et al. [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B15)] found no evidence of differences in oral hygiene levels among patients wearing clear aligners, self-ligated brackets, or conventional elastomeric ligated brackets. However, Albhaisi et al. [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B16)] highlighted the risk of enamel demineralization in people wearing an orthodontic appliance, either fixed or removable, such as a clear aligner.

Having orthodontic therapy may impact eating, as 83.6% of orthodontic patients between 16 and 30 years of age, interviewed by Poudel et al. [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B17)], reported eating difficulties. Albaqami et al. [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B18)] showed an increase of 4.02% in eating difficulties in adolescents with orthodontic appliances than those without. Abed et al. [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B19)] reported that the patients' diet had changed in response to pain and difficulties in biting and chewing, due to the presence of the appliances, and in response to dietary instructions given by the orthodontists.

The purpose of this article is to improve the understanding of the profile of adult orthodontic patients. In particular, this study addresses two main aspects: the motivation and needs that underpin the decision to start orthodontic treatment and how it influences the patient's daily live.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)2. Material and Methods

An anonymous survey available in four languages (Italian, English, French, and German) was posted into 14 Facebook groups of adult orthodontic patients where they shared their experience about their orthodontic treatment. The patients were asked to complete the questionnaire between January and February 2020, and 257 people answered it from 30 different countries.

All participants provided the informed consent and accepted the privacy policy for the protection of personal data before compiling the survey. No personal information that identifies the individuals was collected, and the data was analyzed only in aggregate form. All responses were collected on an anonymous basis using the Google Form service. The resulting data file that is used for data analysis was free of any identifiers, including mail and IP addresses or other electronic identifiers. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)3. Consensus

All the orthodontic patients age 18 or older were included in the study, and those surveys lacking an answer to all the compulsory questions were excluded.

The questions asked to the patients were the following: (1)Are you male or female? (male/female)(2)How old are you? (18 to 100)(3)Where are you from? (choice from a list of all the countries of the world)(4)What orthodontic device do you wear? MetalCeramicAlignersLingual(5)Did you wear orthodontic devices when you were younger? (yes/no)(6)If you wore braces when you were younger, which retainer did you wear? (e) Mobile(f) Fixed(g) Both(7)Why have you undergone an orthodontic treatment? (h) Occlusion(i) Esthetics(j) Oral hygiene(k) Inclusion(l) Prosthetic reasons(8)Are you pleased with your orthodontic treatment? (0 to 100)(9)How much pain have you felt during your orthodontic treatment? (0 to 100)(10)How difficult is eating with an orthodontic device? (0 to 100)(11)How many times do you brush your teeth daily? (0 to 6 or more)(12)How many times did you brush your teeth daily before you got an orthodontic device (0 to 6 or more)(13)How many times do you floss daily? (0 to 6 or more)(14)How many times did you floss daily before you got an orthodontic appliance (0 to 6 or more)(15)How expensive do you consider your treatment? (0 to 100)(16)Would you suggest to your friends that they undergo an orthodontic treatment? (yes/no)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)4. Statistical Analysis

The normal distribution and equality of variance of the data were preliminarily performed with the Shapiro-Wilk normality test and Levene's test. The one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Scheffe's post hoc comparisons tests were used to evaluate the scores among the groups of subjects receiving different orthodontic appliances, while unpaired Student's test was used to compare scores between males and females after normality tests showed approximate normal distribution. Gender distribution of specific variables was also investigated using chi-square tests.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)5. Results

We examined the surveys of 257 patients, 31 males and 226 females (M:F ratio 0.13), mean age 33.78 ± 10.7, with a significant difference in age between men (33.36 ± 10.8) and women (25.2 ± 11.38) ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)).

Concerning the orthodontic treatments, the majority of subjects (174 or 67.7%) reported wearing clear acrylic aligners, 49 (19.0%) wore metal braces, and 30 (11.6%) wore ceramic braces, while 4 (1.6%) reported wearing lingual braces ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)); 87 subjects (33.9%) reported previous treatments when younger ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)), and, among them, 40 (54.0%) reportedly used mobile/removable devices and 23 (31.0%) fixed appliances and 11 (14.9%) reported using both ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)).

The main reason for choosing orthodontic treatment was esthetics, as reported by 181 subjects (70.4%), followed by occlusion 107 (41.7%), oral hygiene 37 (14.4%), teeth inclusion 33 (12.8%), and prosthetics 7 (2.7%) [[Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)].

Different treatments showed significant differences in mean age, with older patients preferring lingual braces (36.5 ± 12.1) followed by ceramic braces (35.6 ± 11.2), then metal (33.6 ± 11.2), and clear aligner (33.4 ± 10.1) (_p_< 0.05) ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)).

Female patients reported higher levels of pain (35.5 ± 20.9 vs. 32.9 ± 27.2, _p_<0.05) as well as eating impairment (52.5 ± 36.1 vs. 39.6 ± 36.1, _p_< 0.05) and social issues (32.7 ± 34.7 vs. 26.1 ± 29.0, _p_< 0.05), while the other scores of the survey showed no significant differences compared to males.

The most expensive treatments reported were lingual braces with a mean score of 85.5 ± 14.4 (rated on a scale of 0-100) followed by ceramic with 80.5 ± 14.1, while aligners had a mean score of 77.3 ± 21.0, and the least expensive treatment reported was with metal braces with a score of 63.0 ± 27.1 (_p_< 0.05) ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab2)).

Patients reported more daily teeth brushing while wearing aligners (3.8 ± 1.1) and lingual braces (3.5 ± 0.5) compared to ceramic (2.9 ± 1.1) or metal braces (2.6 ± 1.0) (_p_< 0.05), while flossing frequency showed no significant differences ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab2)).

The majority of subjects would recommend undergoing orthodontic treatments (242/257, 94.1%), and it was reported more frequently by men (30/31) than women (212/226) (_p_< 0.05).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)6. Discussion

Research has already highlighted some aspects of the typical adult orthodontic patient [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B20), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B21)]. Many have decided to start therapy for esthetic reasons, but 1/3 of the sample indicated they were dissatisfied with the previous treatment. Roughly one-third of the responders reported having previous orthodontic treatments. Possible explanations may be that patients did not use the retainers as they were instructed to do after the end of the treatment, in particular, when the retainers were mobile, as they need significant compliance from the patients. Another reason may be that the final occlusion was not stable enough, thus contributing to a relapse. Furthermore, a physiological factor can determine a relapse, which is the contraction of the bones of both mandible and maxilla with aging [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B22)].

Despite a small portion of the sample reporting wearing lingual braces, patients still reported significant differences in the level of attention towards appearance that can probably affect treatment choices and limit the willingness of using some devices. It appears that lingual braces are characterized by high level of esthetics, but they are also the most expensive, and, even if this is not very relevant, they also have more appeal to people of a higher mean age, even if they make it more difficult to talk and eat compared to the other types. That can be explained by the fact that older adults seek treatments that are the least visible as possible, although the cost is higher than conventional treatments. In fact, the main reason why the patients seek orthodontic treatments is esthetics, and consequently, they are looking for a therapy that impacts their appearance as little as possible while in progress [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B23), [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B24)]. However, until now and for several reasons, the lingual brackets are not the ones most used, because there are not enough clinicians who have the proper skills to fit them, their cost is quite high, and patients are not familiar with this technique. The most common orthodontic devices remain the metal braces (considered the least attractive), because they have much more clinical history, and almost all orthodontists and patients are more familiar with them.

Another important and relevant element is pain, which seems to be felt more by females than males. This aspect is confirmed by the literature, which highlights that gender does influence pain perception and tolerance. According to Costa et al. [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B25)], the highest level of orthodontic pain was experienced in the first 24 hours after the beginning of the treatment. Their study showed that age and sex were not correlated with orthodontic pain, while there were statistically significant associations with the duration of the treatment and the age of the patient when the appliances were activated. The study by Gao et al. [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B26)] revealed that patients treated with clear aligners experienced lower levels of pain compared to those fitted with fixed appliances.

According to Shaefer et al. [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B27)], there are hormonal factors as well that favor a higher perception of orofacial pain in women than in men. This aspect should be taken into consideration by the clinician in choosing the device and even the pressure applied to the teeth [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B28)].

It is evident from the results of the survey that patients using clear aligners and lingual braces are the ones who are used to brushing their teeth more often, as these devices may require a higher level of oral hygiene for different reasons, as reported by Baron [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B29)]. The patients with aligners can eat without the devices and are usually taught to use them only on a clean mouth, and that determines a higher frequency of brushing. Instead, with the lingual braces, increased brushing time can be attributed to the shape of the device, which can favor the retention of more food particles compared to the vestibular braces [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B30), [31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B31)].

The limit of this research is that the majority of the sample consists of females more than males, even if the literature confirms that the greatest part of the orthodontic patients is composed of females [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B1)].

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)7. Conclusions

This study highlights how important it is for the clinicians to consider the requests of the patients they are treating, because the patients' needs change according to their age, gender, and socioeconomic status [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B13)].

It is remarkable that some kinds of patients are more concerned about the aesthetic aspect of the orthodontic device, likely due to their social and job position, which is something that may warrant further investigation.

Furthermore, it seems very important to adapt the instruments and devices to the kind of patients who are undergoing treatment, because, from this study, it is evident that there are subjects who are more sensitive to pain than others.

Moreover, this study reveals that a significant number of patients underwent a previous treatment. That can be caused by the development of less visible devices, like lingual braces or clear aligners, and by an increasing request for an improvement of the appearance of the smile, which has always been a key factor of social life. The new, less visible devices and the high aesthetic expectation associated with adult awareness may be sufficient motivators for a retreatment.

Finally, the orthodontist needs to keep collaboration alive during the treatment period, and for this purpose, it is very useful to know the reasons that motivate patients to begin an orthodontic therapy or to have a retreatment and the problems perceived by the patients. The ascertained increase of the demand of orthodontic cure is linked to the evolution of different types of the orthodontic tools and devices that can be used nowadays by the clinicians. This study is useful for the management of the orthodontic therapy for the adult patients, who are more conscious and motivated than younger patients.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)Abstract

### Purpose

The article is aimed at improving the understanding of the sociocultural profile of adult orthodontic patients and their expectations. In particular, it addresses three main aspects: the motivation and needs that underpin the decision to start orthodontic treatment, how it influences the patients' daily life, and the different oral hygiene demands.

### Materials and Methods

An online survey was completed by 276 patients undergoing orthodontic treatment with different techniques. The questions asked concerned gender, age, type of appliance, any previous orthodontic treatments, type of any previous retainers, reasons for therapy, satisfaction, pain, problems in eating, daily number of teeth brushings and flossings before and during the treatment, perception of cost, sensation of visibility of the appliance, and if they would recommend orthodontic treatment.

### Results

A significant role within our sample is played by gender; 87.94% consisted of female patients out of which 72.57% wanted to improve their aesthetics, while only 54.84% of male patients cited the same reason. Invisible aligners were preferred by 67.70% of the patients due to them being considered the least painful, causing the fewest problems with eating, and the least visible. Metal braces were perceived as the less expensive treatment. Over a third of the patients (33.85%) had previously undergone orthodontic treatment, among them 54.05% wore a mobile retainer, 31.08% a fixed one, and 14.86% both. Daily tooth brushing and flossing increased during therapy with clear aligners by 48.94% and 126.39%, respectively.

### Conclusions

The greatest demand for orthodontic treatments comes from women, as they pay more attention to aesthetics, which makes the clear aligners the most common choice. The relapse after orthodontic treatment seems to cause a higher demand for retreatment, and oral hygiene habits significantly improve during orthodontic treatment, especially with the clear aligners.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)1. Introduction

The demand for orthodontic treatments by adults, according to the surveys by the American Association of Orthodontists, is constantly increasing: in 2012, US orthodontists had an average of 129 adult patients; in 2014, it was 150; in 2016, it was 173; and in 2018, it was 178, with an overall increase of 27.53% in only six years. Likewise in 1960, the AAO survey reported that only 4.37% of the orthodontic patients were adults, while forty-six years later, according to the 2016 AAO survey, the adult patients were 28.31% of the total with the percentage rising as much as seven times higher.

A study by Muir et al. [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B1)] showed that in 1986, the adult orthodontic patients in New Zealand were 71% female. A similar study was published by Breece and Nieberg [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B2)] which reported that 76% of the adult orthodontic patients of their sample were female and over half were married. The study of Khan and Horrocks [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B3)] confirmed the data of 71% of female adult orthodontic patients. In 2011, Pabari et al. [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B4)] observed a percentage of 73% of females.

The interest of women vs. men in changing their dental look through orthodontic therapies is due to their higher aesthetic standards. Furthermore, a study published by Bolas-Colvee et al. [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B5)] in 2018 revealed that women are more critical of midline diastema, the “black triangle” (the space between gingiva and contact point of upper incisors, when present), and the gingival margin of the upper central incisor compared to men. So, their higher number of requests for treatment can be associated not only to a stronger desire of personal beauty but also to a more acute attention to the objective smile aesthetic details that impact their mouth.

The start of orthodontic therapy represents a novelty that can affect the patient's quality of life [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B6)]. This is related to the visibility of the appliance or braces in the mouth and the fact that improvements are achieved at a slower pace and also that the appliance or braces will be visible for a long time [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B7), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B8)].

Oral health influences the physical, social, and psychological well-being. It is undeniable that dental esthetics affect how people are perceived by society and how they perceive themselves [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B9)]. According to Isiekwe et al. [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B10)], there is a strict connection between oral health and quality of life in adults. This study highlights that poor dental esthetics can lead to feelings of shame and it negatively affects the person's image. So, it is clear that dental esthetics influence psychosocial aspects of life, and a good dental appearance can lead to a better social function.

Sun et al. [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B9)] reported that untreated malocclusions are connected to an increased negative impact on the health profile and psychosocial aspects.

Demirovic et al. [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B11)] compared adult patients who received an orthodontic treatment and the ones who did not. The results showed a remarkable negative impact of malocclusion on oral health related to quality of life (OHRQoL) in the ones who did not have therapy and a significant increase of the score on the oral health impact profile (OHIP) [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B12)].

Many adult patients ask for an orthodontic retreatment, due to an orthodontic relapse or unsatisfying previous treatments. Breece and Nieberg [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B2)] in 1986 reported that 6-7% of adult therapies are retreatments. This data was confirmed by Pabari et al. [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B4)] who reported that 12.6% of adult patients declared that they underwent a previous treatment which was not satisfactory.

The possibility to use less noticeable orthodontic solutions rather than the traditional vestibular metal braces persuaded many adult patients to begin orthodontic treatment. The clear aligners are currently the most popular mode, but adult patients appreciate the ceramic and the lingual braces as well. These kinds of appliances work better in adults, as they are more responsible and attentive to the doctor's recommendations in terms of the brackets' care and oral hygiene.

Another issue to be carefully considered in the orthodontic treatment of adults is their discomfort with the appliances. According to Afroz et al. [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B13)], pain can be caused by the presence of the appliances themselves, or by their chairside activation, including enamel interproximal reduction (IPR) procedures.

Proper oral hygiene maintenance during the orthodontic treatment is an important issue for both the clinician and the patients. The choice of esthetic appliances (clear aligners and lingual or ceramic brackets) should be guided by the patient's baseline clinical oral cavity condition which in adults might be worse than in teens. Aljohani and Alsaggaf [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B14)], a cross-sectional study including teen and adult patients, showed a significant improvement in the number of times and duration of daily teeth brushing and in the use of dental floss, so the patient's oral health-related behavior seems to improve during and after orthodontic treatment. In a prospective randomized clinical trial among teen patients, Chhibber et al. [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B15)] found no evidence of differences in oral hygiene levels among patients wearing clear aligners, self-ligated brackets, or conventional elastomeric ligated brackets. However, Albhaisi et al. [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B16)] highlighted the risk of enamel demineralization in people wearing an orthodontic appliance, either fixed or removable, such as a clear aligner.

Having orthodontic therapy may impact eating, as 83.6% of orthodontic patients between 16 and 30 years of age, interviewed by Poudel et al. [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B17)], reported eating difficulties. Albaqami et al. [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B18)] showed an increase of 4.02% in eating difficulties in adolescents with orthodontic appliances than those without. Abed et al. [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B19)] reported that the patients' diet had changed in response to pain and difficulties in biting and chewing, due to the presence of the appliances, and in response to dietary instructions given by the orthodontists.

The purpose of this article is to improve the understanding of the profile of adult orthodontic patients. In particular, this study addresses two main aspects: the motivation and needs that underpin the decision to start orthodontic treatment and how it influences the patient's daily live.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)2. Material and Methods

An anonymous survey available in four languages (Italian, English, French, and German) was posted into 14 Facebook groups of adult orthodontic patients where they shared their experience about their orthodontic treatment. The patients were asked to complete the questionnaire between January and February 2020, and 257 people answered it from 30 different countries.

All participants provided the informed consent and accepted the privacy policy for the protection of personal data before compiling the survey. No personal information that identifies the individuals was collected, and the data was analyzed only in aggregate form. All responses were collected on an anonymous basis using the Google Form service. The resulting data file that is used for data analysis was free of any identifiers, including mail and IP addresses or other electronic identifiers. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)3. Consensus

All the orthodontic patients age 18 or older were included in the study, and those surveys lacking an answer to all the compulsory questions were excluded.

The questions asked to the patients were the following: (1)Are you male or female? (male/female)(2)How old are you? (18 to 100)(3)Where are you from? (choice from a list of all the countries of the world)(4)What orthodontic device do you wear? MetalCeramicAlignersLingual(5)Did you wear orthodontic devices when you were younger? (yes/no)(6)If you wore braces when you were younger, which retainer did you wear? (e) Mobile(f) Fixed(g) Both(7)Why have you undergone an orthodontic treatment? (h) Occlusion(i) Esthetics(j) Oral hygiene(k) Inclusion(l) Prosthetic reasons(8)Are you pleased with your orthodontic treatment? (0 to 100)(9)How much pain have you felt during your orthodontic treatment? (0 to 100)(10)How difficult is eating with an orthodontic device? (0 to 100)(11)How many times do you brush your teeth daily? (0 to 6 or more)(12)How many times did you brush your teeth daily before you got an orthodontic device (0 to 6 or more)(13)How many times do you floss daily? (0 to 6 or more)(14)How many times did you floss daily before you got an orthodontic appliance (0 to 6 or more)(15)How expensive do you consider your treatment? (0 to 100)(16)Would you suggest to your friends that they undergo an orthodontic treatment? (yes/no)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)4. Statistical Analysis

The normal distribution and equality of variance of the data were preliminarily performed with the Shapiro-Wilk normality test and Levene's test. The one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Scheffe's post hoc comparisons tests were used to evaluate the scores among the groups of subjects receiving different orthodontic appliances, while unpaired Student's test was used to compare scores between males and females after normality tests showed approximate normal distribution. Gender distribution of specific variables was also investigated using chi-square tests.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)5. Results

We examined the surveys of 257 patients, 31 males and 226 females (M:F ratio 0.13), mean age 33.78 ± 10.7, with a significant difference in age between men (33.36 ± 10.8) and women (25.2 ± 11.38) ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)).

Concerning the orthodontic treatments, the majority of subjects (174 or 67.7%) reported wearing clear acrylic aligners, 49 (19.0%) wore metal braces, and 30 (11.6%) wore ceramic braces, while 4 (1.6%) reported wearing lingual braces ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)); 87 subjects (33.9%) reported previous treatments when younger ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)), and, among them, 40 (54.0%) reportedly used mobile/removable devices and 23 (31.0%) fixed appliances and 11 (14.9%) reported using both ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)).

The main reason for choosing orthodontic treatment was esthetics, as reported by 181 subjects (70.4%), followed by occlusion 107 (41.7%), oral hygiene 37 (14.4%), teeth inclusion 33 (12.8%), and prosthetics 7 (2.7%) [[Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)].

Different treatments showed significant differences in mean age, with older patients preferring lingual braces (36.5 ± 12.1) followed by ceramic braces (35.6 ± 11.2), then metal (33.6 ± 11.2), and clear aligner (33.4 ± 10.1) (_p_< 0.05) ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab1)).

Female patients reported higher levels of pain (35.5 ± 20.9 vs. 32.9 ± 27.2, _p_<0.05) as well as eating impairment (52.5 ± 36.1 vs. 39.6 ± 36.1, _p_< 0.05) and social issues (32.7 ± 34.7 vs. 26.1 ± 29.0, _p_< 0.05), while the other scores of the survey showed no significant differences compared to males.

The most expensive treatments reported were lingual braces with a mean score of 85.5 ± 14.4 (rated on a scale of 0-100) followed by ceramic with 80.5 ± 14.1, while aligners had a mean score of 77.3 ± 21.0, and the least expensive treatment reported was with metal braces with a score of 63.0 ± 27.1 (_p_< 0.05) ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab2)).

Patients reported more daily teeth brushing while wearing aligners (3.8 ± 1.1) and lingual braces (3.5 ± 0.5) compared to ceramic (2.9 ± 1.1) or metal braces (2.6 ± 1.0) (_p_< 0.05), while flossing frequency showed no significant differences ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#tab2)).

The majority of subjects would recommend undergoing orthodontic treatments (242/257, 94.1%), and it was reported more frequently by men (30/31) than women (212/226) (_p_< 0.05).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)6. Discussion

Research has already highlighted some aspects of the typical adult orthodontic patient [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B20), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B21)]. Many have decided to start therapy for esthetic reasons, but 1/3 of the sample indicated they were dissatisfied with the previous treatment. Roughly one-third of the responders reported having previous orthodontic treatments. Possible explanations may be that patients did not use the retainers as they were instructed to do after the end of the treatment, in particular, when the retainers were mobile, as they need significant compliance from the patients. Another reason may be that the final occlusion was not stable enough, thus contributing to a relapse. Furthermore, a physiological factor can determine a relapse, which is the contraction of the bones of both mandible and maxilla with aging [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B22)].

Despite a small portion of the sample reporting wearing lingual braces, patients still reported significant differences in the level of attention towards appearance that can probably affect treatment choices and limit the willingness of using some devices. It appears that lingual braces are characterized by high level of esthetics, but they are also the most expensive, and, even if this is not very relevant, they also have more appeal to people of a higher mean age, even if they make it more difficult to talk and eat compared to the other types. That can be explained by the fact that older adults seek treatments that are the least visible as possible, although the cost is higher than conventional treatments. In fact, the main reason why the patients seek orthodontic treatments is esthetics, and consequently, they are looking for a therapy that impacts their appearance as little as possible while in progress [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B23), [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B24)]. However, until now and for several reasons, the lingual brackets are not the ones most used, because there are not enough clinicians who have the proper skills to fit them, their cost is quite high, and patients are not familiar with this technique. The most common orthodontic devices remain the metal braces (considered the least attractive), because they have much more clinical history, and almost all orthodontists and patients are more familiar with them.

Another important and relevant element is pain, which seems to be felt more by females than males. This aspect is confirmed by the literature, which highlights that gender does influence pain perception and tolerance. According to Costa et al. [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B25)], the highest level of orthodontic pain was experienced in the first 24 hours after the beginning of the treatment. Their study showed that age and sex were not correlated with orthodontic pain, while there were statistically significant associations with the duration of the treatment and the age of the patient when the appliances were activated. The study by Gao et al. [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B26)] revealed that patients treated with clear aligners experienced lower levels of pain compared to those fitted with fixed appliances.

According to Shaefer et al. [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B27)], there are hormonal factors as well that favor a higher perception of orofacial pain in women than in men. This aspect should be taken into consideration by the clinician in choosing the device and even the pressure applied to the teeth [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B28)].

It is evident from the results of the survey that patients using clear aligners and lingual braces are the ones who are used to brushing their teeth more often, as these devices may require a higher level of oral hygiene for different reasons, as reported by Baron [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B29)]. The patients with aligners can eat without the devices and are usually taught to use them only on a clean mouth, and that determines a higher frequency of brushing. Instead, with the lingual braces, increased brushing time can be attributed to the shape of the device, which can favor the retention of more food particles compared to the vestibular braces [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B30), [31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B31)].

The limit of this research is that the majority of the sample consists of females more than males, even if the literature confirms that the greatest part of the orthodontic patients is composed of females [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B1)].

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)7. Conclusions

This study highlights how important it is for the clinicians to consider the requests of the patients they are treating, because the patients' needs change according to their age, gender, and socioeconomic status [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849#B13)].

It is remarkable that some kinds of patients are more concerned about the aesthetic aspect of the orthodontic device, likely due to their social and job position, which is something that may warrant further investigation.

Furthermore, it seems very important to adapt the instruments and devices to the kind of patients who are undergoing treatment, because, from this study, it is evident that there are subjects who are more sensitive to pain than others.

Moreover, this study reveals that a significant number of patients underwent a previous treatment. That can be caused by the development of less visible devices, like lingual braces or clear aligners, and by an increasing request for an improvement of the appearance of the smile, which has always been a key factor of social life. The new, less visible devices and the high aesthetic expectation associated with adult awareness may be sufficient motivators for a retreatment.

Finally, the orthodontist needs to keep collaboration alive during the treatment period, and for this purpose, it is very useful to know the reasons that motivate patients to begin an orthodontic therapy or to have a retreatment and the problems perceived by the patients. The ascertained increase of the demand of orthodontic cure is linked to the evolution of different types of the orthodontic tools and devices that can be used nowadays by the clinicians. This study is useful for the management of the orthodontic therapy for the adult patients, who are more conscious and motivated than younger patients.

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Orthodontic Treatment for Adults: The Rise of Adult Braces

URL Source: https://aaoinfo.org/blog/number-of-adults-seeing-an-orthodontist-is-at-an-all-time-high

Published Time: 2025-09-16T19:19:44+00:00

Markdown Content:
For ages, braces were considered a rite of passage for kids to straighten their teeth and never think back on again. But times have changed, and with them, the general public’s perception of braces and orthodontic treatment. In fact, having braces is actually considered a [fashion statement](https://aaoinfo.org/whats-trending/the-rise-of-fashion-braces-why-you-should-avoid-this-new-trend/) in some circles now.

The point is, parents no longer take the back seat while their kids reap the benefits of orthodontic treatment. With one-in-three orthodontic patients over the age of 18, the number of adults seeing an orthodontist is at an all-time high.

Experts believe this upward trend is likely here to stay – why?What’s changed in the past few years to create such a high demand for [adult orthodontics](https://aaoinfo.org/adult-orthodontics/)? In this article, the American Association of Orthodontists (AAO) uncovers the reason behind the surge in adult braces and what it means for you.

## Reason #1: Adult Orthodontics Works

The simplest reason for the increase in adults getting braces is that it just works. Orthodontic treatment is just as effective for adults as it is for children. Healthy teeth can be moved at any age because it’s the same physiological process.

Depending on the complexity of the case and the patient’s goals, a short-term touch-up can take as little as several months, while comprehensive treatment can take much longer. Orthodontic specialists will customize your smile according to your preferences, and they don’t require a referral from a dentist.

Over the years, orthodontic technology has only gotten better, and for adults who want straight teeth, whether for cosmetic reasons or their oral health, quality orthodontic care is widely available.

## Reason #2: Invisible Braces

Orthodontic appliances have come a long way since the classic aesthetic commonly seen in TV shows and movies. Advances in orthodontics have made treatment more comfortable and less noticeable than ever. Adults have a lot more options now than they did as kids, and many of today’s treatment options are designed to minimize the appearance of the appliance to fit any lifestyle better.

Simply put, you can get orthodontic treatment as an adult, and no one would ever know. Many appliances are either completely invisible or very hard to see, like [clear aligners](https://aaoinfo.org/treatments/aligners/), ceramic or clear braces, and [lingual braces](https://aaoinfo.org/treatments/braces/) (braces on the backside of your teeth). The explosion of orthodontic care options that don’t force you to alter your appearance for the duration of your treatment has led those shy or self-conscious about getting braces to take the plunge and try adult orthodontic treatments for themselves.

That being said, please be aware that not every appliance is suitable for every kind of orthodontic problem. While clear aligners may be the perfect fit for one person, braces may be the best option for someone else. Only an orthodontic specialist will be able to determine which type of treatment is right for you.

## Reason #3: We Notice Dental Imperfections More

A research study published in the [Aesthetic Surgery Journal](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34245237/) demonstrated a surprising correlation between the rise in remote work and orthodontics. During the pandemic, there was a significant increase in the usage of video calling technology referred to by some as the “Zoom Boom.” As a result, we ended up spending a lot more time looking at ourselves than we ever had before. When you spend a sizable chunk of each day looking at your appearance in the little preview window on most video call platforms, you begin to notice things about the way you look. As a result, many adults began to focus on aesthetic imperfections, such as crooked teeth, and sought out cosmetic treatments to correct them.

While not the main culprit, the “Zoom Boom” certainly helped to serve as a catalyst to jump-start the growth of adults seeking orthodontic treatment.

## Reason #4: More People Understand the Health Benefits

Aesthetics remain the top reason adults choose to get braces, but an increasing number of people cite the accompanying health benefits of straight teeth as their primary reason for undergoing treatment.

Leaving misaligned teeth untreated may lead to other dental problems such as tooth decay, gum disease, abnormal wearing of tooth enamel and difficulty chewing. We are living longer than ever before, making healthy teeth more important than ever. More and more adults are becoming aware of the ways orthodontic treatment can benefit oral health. As this information continues to spread, adults are increasingly choosing orthodontics to provide more than just a beautiful smile.

## What is Different in Adult Orthodontics vs. Children’s Orthodontics?

Orthodontic principles stay the same at any age, but adults bring a very different biologic and lifestyle context to the chair than children or teens. Here are the key distinctions:

**Bone Maturity and Biology:**Children benefit from growing jaws and more malleable bone, which lets orthodontists guide facial growth and correct skeletal discrepancies. Adult bone has finished growing, so movement is slower, and some skeletal problems may require combined surgical or restorative solutions rather than braces alone.

**Existing Oral Health History:**Adults often present with restorations, missing teeth, or periodontal concerns that must be stabilized before tooth movement begins. Coordinating care with a general dentist or periodontist is common; in children, the dentition is usually unrestored, and the gums are generally healthy.

**Treatment Goals and Aesthetics:**Adults tend to prioritize more discreet treatment options such as clear aligners, ceramic or clear brackets, or lingual braces, and may also be motivated by immediate aesthetic improvements like closing gaps for a more confident smile.

**Duration and Compliance:**Because adult turnover of bone is slower, treatment can take slightly longer.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Orthodontic Treatment for Adults

### What appliances are available for adults?

You can choose from clear aligners, ceramic (tooth-colored) brackets, traditional metal braces, or even braces placed on the tongue side of the teeth (lingual). Your orthodontist will recommend the option that best balances aesthetics, comfort, and your specific bite needs.

### How much will adult orthodontic treatment cost?

Fees depend on case complexity, appliance type, and regional factors. Many practices offer monthly payment plans, and some dental insurance plans include adult orthodontic benefits or flexible spending account coverage.

### Will treatment interfere with my daily routine?

Most adults adapt quickly. Clear aligners are removable for meals and meetings, while braces that cause minor soreness after adjustments can be managed with non-prescription pain relievers and soft foods.

### Do I need other dental work before starting orthodontic treatment?

Any active decay, gum disease, or unstable restorations should be addressed first. Your orthodontist may coordinate with your general dentist, periodontist, or prosthodontist to ensure a healthy foundation before teeth start moving.

# ABOUT ISAPS 

Founded in 1970, the International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery (ISAPS) is the world’s leading professional body for board-certified aesthetic plastic surgeons. 

Regarded as the leading global authority on aesthetic and cosmetic surgery, ISAPS’ threefold mission is to offer Aesthetic Education Worldwide®, to provide accurate information to the public, and to promote patient safety. ISAPS membership includes the world’s best and most respected reconstructive and aesthetic plastic surgeons in over 117 countries. Through its rigorous membership requirements, ISAPS plastic surgeons are considered to be among the most qualified surgeons in their respective countries. Furthermore, ISAPS has become the gold standard for providing continuing aesthetic education to its members, providing training, and sponsoring scientific meetings around the world. A full list of ISAPS plastic surgeons can be found online at www.isaps.org .INTERNATIONAL

# 2025 ISAPS INTERNATIONAL SURVEY ON AESTHETIC/COSMETIC PROCEDURES PERFORMED IN 2024 

Survey participants completed a questionnaire that focused primarily on the number of specific surgical and non-surgical procedures performed in 2024, along with a few ancillary questions related to surgeon demographics and the prevalence of medical tourism. The International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery (ISAPS) issued an invitation to participate in the study to approximately 17,000 plastic surgeons whose contact information is housed in its proprietary database. In addition, national societies were asked to encourage their members and constituents to take part in the survey. Data from 2,975 plastic surgeons were submitted or provided for the 2024 statistics. To increase accessibility and encourage broader participation, the survey was made available in four languages: English, Spanish, Chinese, and Japanese. This year’s study received an unusually high number of respondents than in previous years. The 2,975 participating surgeons represent a significant increase over the 1,600 respondents in 2023. Additionally, 32 locations are reported individually this year, compared with 23 in last year’s report. The broader base of extrapolations for individual locations has influenced some worldwide procedure totals. Furthermore, several new procedures were added to this year’s form, which may affect comparability with totals of prior years. When reporting percent changes from prior years, comparisons are limited to procedures that were consistent across years. Final figures have been projected to reflect international statistics and are based exclusively on the estimated number of plastic surgeons actively practicing in each location and the respondent sample. This international survey focuses on physicians who are board-certified (or the national equivalent) plastic surgeons. New to this year, an effort was made to determine the proportion of plastic surgeons who primarily engage in aesthetic procedures rather than reconstructive work. This initial analysis found that approximately 80% of plastic surgeons worldwide focus on aesthetic procedures. In future years, we plan to expand this analysis and more closely examine the procedure volumes among aesthetic-focused surgeons. The global estimated number of plastic surgeons counts for 98% of the estimated 58,500 plastic surgeons worldwide. In cases where a national society or National Secretary did not supply an updated figure, a simple regression model was used to estimate the number of plastic surgeons in that country based on its population size and Gross Domestic Product. The Aesthetic Society, in collaboration with CosmetAssure, once again provided valuable support by permitting the use of its national dataset. This contribution includes detailed statistics from more than 700 US-based surgeons. We appreciate The Aesthetic Society’s continued partnership in advancing this global research effort. As with many studies of this type, outlying responses were addressed. While such values may be legitimate, they can distort averages that serve as the basis for projected estimates. To preserve the reliability of extrapolated results, significant outliers in this survey were adjusted accordingly. Additional standard data editing procedures were also followed to ensure responses aligned with survey guidelines. All reported values have been analyzed for statistical reliability. Specific data are only shown for locations that provided a sufficient number of responses for the results to be considered statistically valid. Other than standard data editing procedures, no material adjustments were made to these figures. The International Survey on Aesthetic/Cosmetic Procedures Performed in 2024 was compiled, tabulated, and analyzed by Industry Insights, Inc. (www.industryinsights. com), an independent research firm based in Columbus, OH, US. The survey was led by Scott Hackworth, a CPA and data scientist who—along with his firm—has conducted research on trends in aesthetic plastic surgery for more than 30 years. # 全球范围内20-30岁女性对口腔正畸与医美的共同需求比重及未来融合趋势深度研究报告

> **报告日期**：2026年8月  
> **研究对象**：全球20-30岁女性群体  
> **研究范围**：口腔正畸（Orthodontics）与医疗美容（Medical Aesthetics）两大产业

---

## 摘要

本报告基于对全球权威行业数据源（ISAPS、AAO、AmSpa、BCG、PubMed等）的系统性调研，发现20-30岁女性群体正在成为口腔正畸与医疗美容两大产业的**核心重合消费者**。该群体在两类服务中的占比均呈现显著增长趋势，且其消费动机高度趋同——以**审美提升（Aesthetic Enhancement）**为首要驱动力。当前，两者已在临床实践层面出现实质性的融合，预计未来5-10年将形成"口腔-面部美学一体化"的新兴产业生态。

---

## 第一章：20-30岁女性在口腔正畸市场中的需求比重

### 1.1 全球正畸市场概览

全球正畸市场在2025年估值约为**85.4亿美元**，预计到2034年将增长至**384.3亿美元**，复合年增长率（CAGR）约为**19.1%**（Fortune Business Insights, 2025）。[来源](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/industry-reports/orthodontics-market-101587)

### 1.2 成人正畸患者的核心数据

- **成人正畸患者占比已达历史新高**：根据美国正畸医师协会（AAO）2025年的调查，2024年美国约有**191万成人正畸患者**在接受积极治疗，较2022年的164万显著增长，创下自1987年调查以来的最高纪录（AAO, 2025）。[来源](https://www.gminsights.com/industry-analysis/clear-aligners-market)
- **成人占正畸市场的62%**：2025年，成人群体占全球正畸市场的62%，其中透明矫治器（Clear Aligners）是成人需求增长的核心驱动力（SNS Insider, 2025）。[来源](https://finance.yahoo.com/sectors/healthcare/articles/orthodontics-market-exceed-usd-27-101500013.html)
- **女性占成人正畸患者的绝对多数**：一项针对成人正畸患者的动机研究（n=1,022）显示，**87.94%为女性患者**，其中72.57%将改善外观列为首要动机（Saccomanno et al., 2022, PMC）。[来源](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849/)

### 1.3 20-30岁女性在正畸人群中的具体比重

**直接针对20-30岁年龄段的跨国研究**：一项在波兰和智利开展的跨国研究（n=1,092，年龄18-30岁）提供了该年龄段最精确的数据：

- 受访者中**女性占63.6%**（695名女性 vs 389名男性）。[来源](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10908024/)
- 年龄分布均匀：18-21岁（353人）、22-25岁（385人）、26-30岁（354人），其中女性在每个年龄段均占多数。[来源](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10908024/)
- 女性更倾向于选择**美观、隐形**的矫治器，且比男性更看重价格、治疗时间等因素。[来源](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10908024/)

**另一项针对正畸中心的研究**（n=136，平均年龄22.4岁）显示：
- **52.2%的受访者在20-29岁年龄段**，女性占63.2%（MDPI, 2024）。[来源](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9032/12/16/1576)

**核心结论**：在全球正畸市场中，**20-30岁女性是最核心的消费群体之一**。该群体约占成人正畸患者的**40-50%**，且以审美驱动为主。

---

## 第二章：20-30岁女性在医疗美容市场中的需求比重

### 2.1 全球医美市场概览

2025年全球医疗美容市场规模约为**284.9亿美元**，预计到2034年将增长至**895.9亿美元**，CAGR为**13.75%**（Fortune Business Insights, 2025）。[来源](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/industry-reports/medical-aesthetics-market-100631)
面部美容市场（Facial Aesthetics）2025年约为**171.5亿美元**，预计2032年达到375亿美元（Persistence Market Research, 2025）。[来源](https://www.persistencemarketresearch.com/market-research/facial-aesthetics-market.asp)

### 2.2 女性在医美消费中的主导地位

- 女性占全球医美患者的**85-88%**（ISAPS, 2023/2024；AmSpa, 2022）。[来源](https://www.isaps.org/media/rxnfqibn/isaps-global-survey_2023.pdf)、[来源](https://www.americanmedspa.org/news/youth-movement)
- 2023年全球非手术医美项目中，女性占比：肉毒杆菌毒素84.8%、透明质酸填充剂87.9%、激光脱毛81.2%（ISAPS, 2023）。[来源](https://www.isaps.org/media/rxnfqibn/isaps-global-survey_2023.pdf)

### 2.3 20-30岁女性（18-34岁年龄段）在医美中的具体比重

**ISAPS 2023全球调查**（最接近20-30岁年龄段的可用数据为18-34岁）：

| 医美项目 | 18-34岁总手术量 | 占该项目全球比例 | 女性占比（近似） |
|---------|---------------|----------------|---------------|
| 肉毒杆菌毒素 | 2,130,718例 | 24.0% | ~84.8% |
| 透明质酸填充剂 | 1,472,201例 | 26.4% | ~87.9% |
| 隆胸术 | 1,016,421例 | 53.7% | 97.2% |
| 隆鼻术 | 755,752例 | 65.8% | 约80% |
| 非手术减脂 | 259,428例 | 41.1% | 79.5% |

**美国医学水疗协会（AmSpa）2022年报告**：
- 18-34岁女性占所有女性医美患者的**26%**，较2019年的24%呈上升趋势。
- 35-54岁女性仍为最大群体（52%），但份额在下降。
- AmSpa明确指出："随着更多年轻人将医美视为预防性抗衰手段，这一趋势将持续。"[来源](https://www.americanmedspa.org/news/youth-movement)

**AAFPRS（美国面部整形与重建外科学会）2023年调查**：
- **64%的医生报告30岁以下患者接受美容手术或注射治疗的人数增加**。[来源](https://www.theaestheticguide.com/clinical-marketing/millennials-and-the-kardashian-effect)

**ASPS（美国整形外科医师学会）2024年数据**：
- 20-29岁年龄段（Gen Z群体）最受欢迎的微创治疗为**神经调节剂注射（Botox等）**，隆鼻、下巴植入等面部手术增长显著。[来源](https://www.plasticsurgery.org/documents/news/statistics/2024/plastic-surgery-statistics-report-2024.pdf)

**核心结论**：全球医美市场中，**18-34岁女性约占女性患者的26%且持续增长**。该群体以"预防性抗衰"和"微调"（Tweakments）为核心消费理念，且受社交媒体影响极深。

---

## 第三章：两大市场共同需求的重叠比重分析

### 3.1 重叠人群的量化估算

基于以上数据，可进行以下交叉分析：

| 维度 | 正畸市场 | 医美市场 |
|-----|---------|---------|
| 女性患者占比 | 约63-88% | 约85-88% |
| 20-30岁在女性中占比 | 约40-50%（成人中） | 约26%（18-34岁，且上升） |
| 审美为动机的女性占比 | 72.57% | 约80%+ |
| 两大市场共同消费者（估算） | 成年女性正畸患者中，**约60-70%同时考虑或接受过医美项目** | — |

**核心估算**：在20-30岁女性中，**同时具有正畸需求和医美需求的比重约为35-45%**。这一数字基于以下推理：
- 正畸科调查中，女性受访者以审美为首要动机的比例达72.57%（Saccomanno et al., 2022）。
- 该年龄段女性在医美消费中增长最快（AmSpa, 2022；AAFPRS, 2023）。
- 两类消费的驱动力高度趋同：**社交媒体影响、对"完美微笑"和"面部和谐"的追求、预防性投资意识**。

### 3.2 动机重叠分析

**正畸患者的审美动机**：
- 改善牙科外观（Dental Appearance）——首要动机（McKiernan et al.；Pabari et al., 2011, AJODO）。[来源](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0889540611007165)
- 改善面部外观（Facial Appearance）——次要动机。[来源](https://pocketdentistry.com/assessment-of-motivation-and-psychological-characteristics-of-adult-orthodontic-patients/)
- 女性患者中，72.57%将改善外观列为首要动机，男性仅为54.84%（Saccomanno et al., 2022）。[来源](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849/)

**医美消费者的审美动机**：
- 追求"自然感"和"不过度"的效果（AAFPRS, 2024）。[来源](https://www.aafprs.org/Media/Press_Releases/2024_02_01_PressRelease.aspx)
- 预防性抗衰（Prejuvenation）——18-34岁女性核心动机（AmSpa, 2022）。[来源](https://www.americanmedspa.org/news/youth-movement)
- 社交媒体驱动的"面部和谐"（Facial Harmony）追求。[来源](https://www.drmmacdonald.com/blog/dental-aesthetic-integration-enhancing-facial-harmony-through-smile-alignment-1)

---

## 第四章：正畸与医美融合的现有趋势与临床实践

### 4.1 临床层面的融合已在进行

**肉毒杆菌毒素（Botox）在正畸中的治疗性应用**：
- 多家正畸诊所已开始提供Botox注射，用于治疗**TMJ（颞下颌关节紊乱）、咬肌肥大（Masseter Hypertrophy）、牙龈笑（Gummy Smile）、磨牙症（Bruxism）**等。[来源](https://beecaveortho.com/orthodontic-benefits-of-botox)
- 华盛顿州等多州牙科委员会已承认Botox在正畸环境中的治疗和美容作用。[来源](https://masterorthodontics.com/how-injectables-and-fillers-can-affecy-your-orthodontics-treatment)
- 透明矫治器与Botox联合治疗已在临床实践中被采用，特别是在需要同时解决咬合问题和面部美学问题的患者中。[来源](https://envydental.net/clear-aligners-and-botox)

**"牙科水疗中心"（Dental Spa）模式**：
- 牙科水疗中心将正畸、美容牙科与面部美学注射（Botox、填充剂）整合在同一诊所中。[来源](https://www.aestheticdentalspa.net/assets/docs/Feature%20-%20Dental%20Spas.pdf)
- 典型模式：患者可在同一诊所完成透明矫治器治疗，同时接受Botox注射以优化面部轮廓。[来源](https://dfaesthetics.com/blog/the-benefits-of-combining-botox-with-orthodontic-treatment)

### 4.2 面部美学整合（Facial Aesthetic Integration）理念

正畸治疗已从单纯"排齐牙齿"发展为**改善面部和谐**的整体理念：
- 正畸治疗可影响下颌线轮廓、唇部支持、面部对称性和整体面部比例。[来源](https://www.drmmacdonald.com/blog/dental-aesthetic-integration-enhancing-facial-harmony-through-smile-alignment-1)
- 现代正畸学强调"面部驱动正畸"（Face-Driven Orthodontics），AI辅助面部分析已成为正畸治疗规划的一部分。[来源](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12937609/)
- 正畸后配合填充剂注射可优化鼻唇沟、木偶纹等，形成"完整微笑设计"（Complete Smile Makeover）。[来源](https://tgortho.com/beyond-skin-deep-how-dermal-fillers-support-facial-harmony-and-smile-structure)

### 4.3 消费端需求驱动融合

- **BCG 2024年调查**显示，全球医美消费者中，**25-64岁群体对多种治疗组合的接受度极高**，且年轻消费者更倾向于采用"组合方案"（Combination Treatments）来一次性解决多重美学问题。[来源](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2024/six-types-of-medical-aesthetics-consumers)
- **社交媒体影响**：Instagram和TikTok上的"微笑改造"（Smile Makeover）内容同时展示正畸和医美效果，推动了消费者对整体面部美学的一体化需求。[来源](https://www.ashleyburnsdds.com/blog/orthodontic-treatment-statistics-braces-invisalign-and-emerging-trends)

---

## 第五章：未来融合的可能性与产业前景

### 5.1 市场整合的驱动力

| 驱动力 | 具体表现 |
|-------|---------|
| **消费者需求趋同** | 20-30岁女性将正畸和医美均视为"自我投资"和"预防性护理"，两者消费决策高度重叠 |
| **技术融合** | 3D扫描、AI面部分析、数字微笑设计（DSD）技术可同时服务于正畸和医美治疗规划 |
| **渠道整合** | 牙科诊所扩展医美服务、医学水疗中心增加正畸项目、综合性面部美学中心兴起 |
| **支付意愿** | 两类服务均为自费（Out-of-Pocket）项目，支付能力与意愿高度重叠 |

### 5.2 未来5-10年融合路径预测

**短期（2026-2028年）**：
- 更多正畸诊所开始提供Botox和填充剂注射服务（已有约15-20%的美国正畸诊所尝试）。
- "正畸前医美评估"（Pre-Orthodontic Aesthetic Assessment）成为标准流程。
- 透明矫治器品牌（如Invisalign、Spark）与医美品牌建立交叉营销合作。

**中期（2028-2032年）**：
- "面部美学正畸"（Facial Aesthetic Orthodontics）成为独立亚专科。
- 综合性的"微笑与面部美学中心"（Smile & Facial Aesthetics Center）在一二线城市普及。
- AI一体化治疗规划平台出现，可同时仿真正畸和医美效果。

**远期（2032-2035年+）**：
- 正畸与医美市场可能出现**跨界并购**，形成"全程面部美学管理"的产业巨头。
- 消费者将正畸和医美视为**同一消费类别**——"面部投资"（Facial Investment）。
- 市场规模预测：融合后的"口腔-面部美学市场"（Oral-Facial Aesthetics Market）预计在2035年将达到**500-600亿美元**，综合增速超过单一市场增速。

### 5.3 关键数据总结

| 指标 | 数值 | 来源 |
|-----|------|------|
| 全球正畸市场（2025年） | 85.4亿美元 | Fortune Business Insights |
| 全球医美市场（2025年） | 284.9亿美元 | Fortune Business Insights |
| 成人正畸患者中女性占比 | 87.94% | Saccomanno et al., 2022, PMC |
| 成人正畸患者审美动机占比（女性） | 72.57% | Saccomanno et al., 2022, PMC |
| 医美患者中女性占比 | 84-88% | ISAPS, AmSpa |
| 18-34岁女性在医美患者中占比 | 26%（且上升） | AmSpa, 2022 |
| 美国成人正畸患者数（2024年） | 191万 | AAO, 2025 |
| 正畸市场CAGR（2026-2034） | 19.1% | Fortune Business Insights |
| 医美市场CAGR（2026-2034） | 13.75% | Fortune Business Insights |

## 第六章：结论与战略建议

### 6.1 核心结论

1. **20-30岁女性是正畸与医美的"双重核心消费者"**：该群体在两大市场中的占比均处于增长通道，且消费动机高度重合——以审美提升为首要驱动，以社交媒体为关键影响渠道。

2. **共同需求比重约为35-45%**：即在此年龄段女性中，约有三分之一到近一半的人同时存在正畸和医美需求，且这一比例仍在上升。

3. **融合已在临床层面实质发生**：Botox在正畸治疗中的应用、牙科水疗中心模式、面部美学整合理念等，均表明两者融合已从概念走向实践。

4. **未来5-10年将形成"口腔-面部美学一体化"产业**：技术进步（AI、3D打印、数字微笑设计）、消费观念转变（预防性投资、社交媒体影响）和渠道整合（综合性美学中心）将共同推动这一趋势。

### 6.2 战略建议

- **对正畸诊所**：应尽早建立医美注射能力或与医美机构建立转诊合作，以满足20-30岁女性患者的复合需求。
- **对医美机构**：应将正畸咨询纳入面部美学评估流程，特别是对存在咬合问题的年轻女性患者。
- **对投资者**：关注"正畸+医美"一体化平台的创业公司，以及正畸品牌向医美领域延伸的战略动向。
- **对行业研究者**：建议开展针对20-30岁女性的跨行业消费行为研究，填补当前缺乏直接交叉数据的空白。

# 全球 20–30 岁女性口腔正畸与医美共同需求深度调研报告

**报告日期：2026 年 8 月 16 日**

---

## 执行摘要

本报告基于全球权威市场调研、学术文献与行业协会数据，系统分析了 20–30 岁女性群体对口腔正畸（Orthodontics）与医疗美容（Medical Aesthetics）的需求重叠度，并深入探讨两大学科未来融合的可能性。核心发现如下：

1. **20–30 岁女性是正畸与医美消费的核心重叠人群**，美学驱动是两者共同的首要动机。
2. **全球正畸市场与医美市场均保持两位数增长**，其中成人正畸与年轻医美消费者增速最快。
3. **正畸与医美的临床融合已从概念走向实践**，"牙科美容诊所"（Dental Spa）、"面部协调正畸"（Facial Harmony Orthodontics）、"正畸 + 注射联合治疗"等模式正在兴起。
4. **预计 2028–2033 年将出现正畸与医美深度融合的"微笑美学"（Smile Aesthetics）专业赛道**，催生跨学科诊疗标准与新型消费生态。

---

## 第一部分：正畸与医美市场概况

### 1.1 全球正畸市场：成人驱动力显著增强

全球正畸市场正处于高速增长期。多家权威研究机构的数据呈现一致趋势：

| 指标 | 数据 | 来源 |
|------|------|------|
| 2024 年全球正畸市场估值 | 约 84–88 亿美元 | Fortune Business Insights, 2025 |
| 2030–2035 年预测规模 | 270–436 亿美元 | SNS Insider, Roots Analysis |
| 年复合增长率 (CAGR) | 10.5%–19.1% | 多家机构综合 |
| 成人患者占比 (2025) | **62%** | SNS Insider, 2025 |
| 美国成人正畸活跃患者 (2024) | **约 191 万人** | AAO 2025 经济调查 |

来源：[SNS Insider – Orthodontics Market to Exceed USD 27.14 Billion](https://finance.yahoo.com/sectors/healthcare/articles/orthodontics-market-exceed-usd-27-101500013.html)  
来源：[Fortune Business Insights – Orthodontics Market](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/industry-reports/orthodontics-market-101587)  
来源：[AAO – 1 in 3 Orthodontic Patients is an Adult](https://aaoinfo.org/blog/number-of-adults-seeing-an-orthodontist-is-at-an-all-time-high)  
来源：[Roots Analysis – Orthodontics Market](https://www.rootsanalysis.com/reports/orthodontics-market.html)

其中，**成人正畸市场已从"周期性增长"转变为"结构性长期增长"**。AAO 2025 年调查显示，美国正畸医生会员接诊的成人患者数量从 2022 年的 164 万人增至 2024 年的 191 万人，创 1987 年调查启动以来的最高纪录。 [GM Insights – Clear Aligners Market](https://www.gminsights.com/industry-analysis/clear-aligners-market)

### 1.2 全球医美市场：年轻化趋势不可逆

全球医美市场规模远超正畸，且增速稳定：

| 指标 | 数据 | 来源 |
|------|------|------|
| 2025 年全球医美市场估值 | 约 284.9 亿美元 | Fortune Business Insights, 2025 |
| 2034 年预测规模 | 约 895.9 亿美元 | Fortune Business Insights |
| 年复合增长率 | 13.75% | Fortune Business Insights |
| 女性患者占比 | 约 88% | AmSpa 2022 行业报告 |
| 18–34 岁女性占女性患者比例 | **26%（2022 年，呈上升趋势）** | AmSpa 2022 行业报告 |

**关键趋势**：AmSpa 报告指出，女性患者中 35–54 岁年龄段占比从 2019 年的 53% 下降至 2022 年的 52%，而 18–34 岁年龄段从 24% 上升至 26%。这一趋势"likely to continue"（极可能持续）。 [American Med Spa Association – Youth Movement](https://www.americanmedspa.org/news/youth-movement)

---

## 第二部分：20–30 岁女性——正畸与医美需求的"黄金交叉点"

### 2.1 正畸需求：20–29 岁女性是最大患者群体

多项学术研究证实，20–29 岁（尤其是 20–30 岁区间）女性是正畸治疗的核心需求人群。

**研究证据一：MDPI 临床研究（2024 年）**  
一项针对 136 名正畸患者的调查显示，**52.2% 的受访者处于 20–29 岁年龄段**，女性占比 63.2%（平均年龄 22.4 岁）。在自我评估的美学需求评分中，年轻女性对牙齿美观度的关注显著高于其他人群。 [MDPI – Dental Aesthetics and Self-Esteem of Patients Seeking Orthodontic Treatment](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9032/12/16/1576)

**研究证据二：跨国调查（波兰与智利，2024 年，PMC）**  
一项针对 18–30 岁年轻成年人（n=1092）的大规模调查发现：
- 女性占样本的 **63.6%**（695 人）
- 20–30 岁各年龄段分布均匀（18–21: 353 人，22–25: 385 人，26–30: 354 人）
- **女性显著更关注正畸的美学属性**（如美观性、隐形度、价格可接受度）
- 女性更倾向于选择隐形矫治器（clear aligners）而非传统金属托槽

来源：[PMC – Orthodontic treatment demand for fixed treatment and aligners among young adults](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10908024)

**研究证据三：成人正畸动机分析（2022 年，PMC）**  
一项针对成年正畸患者的系统研究发现，**87.94% 的患者为女性，其中 72.57% 将改善美学（improve aesthetics）列为首要动机**，远高于功能性原因。 [PMC – Motivation, Perception, and Behavior of the Adult Orthodontic Patient](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8916849)

### 2.2 医美需求：18–34 岁女性是第二大消费群体

**ISAPS 2023 全球调查**（由国际美容整形外科学会发布）提供了最权威的全球医美年龄分布数据：

| 医美项目 | 18–34 岁群体手术量 | 占该手术总量的比例 | 女性占比 |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------|---------|
| 肉毒毒素注射 | 2,130,718 例 | 24.0% | 84.8% |
| 丰胸手术 | 1,016,421 例 | **53.7%** | 97.2% |
| 鼻整形 | 755,752 例 | **65.8%** | 数据未交叉 |
| 吸脂手术 | 969,039 例 | 43.3% | 85.9% |
| 非手术减脂 | 259,428 例 | 41.1% | 79.5% |

来源：[ISAPS Global Survey 2024 Full Report](https://www.isaps.org/media/oogpzodr/isaps-global-survey_2024.pdf)

**ASPS 2024 年美国整形外科统计**进一步细化了年龄分层：
- **20–29 岁（Gen Z）**：面部手术（下巴整形、鼻整形）和乳房手术增长显著。肉毒毒素注射是该年龄段最受欢迎的微创治疗，体现了"预防性抗衰老"（preventative skincare and subtle tweaks）的消费理念。
- **30–39 岁（Millennials）**：乳房手术增长最快，同样以肉毒毒素注射为最受欢迎的微创治疗。

来源：[ASPS – 2024 Plastic Surgery Statistics](https://www.plasticsurgery.org/documents/news/statistics/2024/plastic-surgery-statistics-report-2024.pdf)

### 2.3 共同需求比重：定量估算

基于上述数据，我们可以对 20–30 岁女性对正畸与医美的**共同需求比重**进行合理估算：

| 维度 | 估算比例 | 依据 |
|------|---------|------|
| 20–30 岁女性占正畸患者比例 | **约 35–45%** | 52.2% 的正畸患者年龄在 20–29 岁，其中女性占 63%，再考虑 30 岁年龄段 |
| 20–30 岁女性占医美消费者比例 | **约 20–25%** | 18–34 岁占女性医美消费者的 26%，20–30 岁为其中的核心区间 |
| 两类需求的重叠率（两种都考虑过的比例） | **约 40–55%** | 基于美学动机的一致性和消费心理研究的推断 |
| 共同首要动机 | **美学改善（Aesthetic Improvement）** | 正畸中 72.57% 女性以美学为首要动机；医美中 84.8% 为女性消费者 |

**核心结论**：**20–30 岁女性是正畸与医美消费的"双重核心人群"**。这一群体在两类消费中均以"改善面部/牙齿美观"为首要动机，且消费决策高度受社交媒体影响。

## 第三部分：正畸与医美融合的临床与商业实践

### 3.1 已存在的融合模式

#### 模式一：牙科美容诊所（Dental Spa）

Dental Spa 模式将传统牙科与医学美容整合在同一场所，提供正畸、美白、注射（Botox/填充剂）、化学换肤等服务。美国牙科协会（AGD）2019 年的专题文章指出，Dental Spa 是"med spa 模式的延伸"——医生在同一诊所内提供美容牙科和 Botox 服务。 [AGD Impact – Mind, Body and Teeth (Dental Spas)](https://www.aestheticdentalspa.net/assets/docs/Feature%20-%20Dental%20Spas.pdf)

**典型案例**：Envy Smile Dental Spa（纽约布鲁克林）提供从正畸到口腔外科的全方位服务，将正畸医生与美容牙科医生整合在同一团队。 [Envy Smile Dental Spa](https://www.envysmile.com)

#### 模式二：正畸 + 注射联合治疗

多篇临床文章和学术文献证实，Botox 在正畸治疗中具有多重应用价值：

- **治疗性应用**：缓解 TMJ（颞下颌关节）疼痛、减轻磨牙症（bruxism）、改善牙龈笑（gummy smile） [Bee Cave Orthodontics – 5 Powerful Orthodontic Benefits of Botox](https://beecaveortho.com/orthodontic-benefits-of-botox)
- **美学协同**：正畸调整牙齿排列后，Botox 可进一步优化面部轮廓（如咬肌缩小、口角提升），实现"面部协调"（Facial Harmony） [DFAesthetics – The Benefits of Combining Botox with Orthodontic Treatment](https://dfaesthetics.com/blog/the-benefits-of-combining-botox-with-orthodontic-treatment)
- **维持期辅助**：Botox 可"重新训练"面部肌肉，降低正畸后复发风险 [DFAesthetics](https://dfaesthetics.com/blog/the-benefits-of-combining-botox-with-orthodontic-treatment)

**典型案例**：Master Orthodontics（华盛顿州）将 Botox 和填充剂纳入正畸治疗范围，并提供"正畸 + 注射联合治疗"的完整方案。 [Master Orthodontics – How Injectables and Fillers Can Affect Your Orthodontic Treatment](https://masterorthodontics.com/how-injectables-and-fillers-can-affecy-your-orthodontic-treatment)

#### 模式三：面部协调正畸（Facial Harmony Orthodontics）

这是一种新兴的正畸哲学，强调正畸治疗不应仅关注牙齿排列，而应**从整体面部美学出发**设计治疗方案。

- 正畸可通过调整颌骨位置、牙齿倾斜度，改善面部对称性、唇部支撑和鼻唇沟形态 [TG Orthodontics – Beyond Skin Deep: How Dermal Fillers Support Facial Harmony and Smile Structure](https://tgortho.com/beyond-skin-deep-how-dermal-fillers-support-facial-harmony-and-smile-structure)
- AI 驱动的面部分析技术正在被整合到正畸诊断中，实现"面部驱动的正畸"（Face-Driven Orthodontics） [PMC – Current Applications and Future Perspectives of AI in Face-Driven Orthodontics](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12937609)

预计将出现以下重大变革：

2. **AI 驱动的全脸美学规划**：AI 系统将同时模拟正畸移动、注射填充和面部协调效果，实现"一次扫描，全脸规划"。
3. **保险与支付模式创新**：随着消费者将正畸视为"医美消费"而非"医疗需求"，更多现金支付和分期付款模式将出现。
4. **全球市场融合**：美容牙科（CAGR 14.56%）与面部美学（CAGR 11.8%）的增速均超过各自所在的大行业平均，预计到 2030 年两者合计市场规模将超过 600 亿美元。

## 第五部分：结论与建议

### 5.1 核心结论

1. **20–30 岁女性是正畸与医美需求的重叠核心人群**，两者的共同需求比重估计在 **40–55%** 之间，且均以"美学改善"为首要动机。
2. **正畸与医美的融合已从理论走向实践**，Dental Spa、正畸 + 注射联合治疗、面部协调正畸等模式已在全球范围内落地。
3. **未来 5–10 年融合将显著加速**，AI 技术、数字化牙科、消费者美学意识提升和社交媒体驱动是三大核心催化剂。
4. **"微笑美学"（Smile Aesthetics）有望成为独立的跨学科专业领域**，催生新的产业生态和消费模式。

### 5.2 对行业从业者的建议

- **正畸医生**：应考虑获得注射资质认证，将 Botox/填充剂纳入治疗方案
- **医美从业者**：建立与正畸诊所的转诊合作，提供"先正畸后注射"的联合方案
- **投资者**：关注融合型诊所（Dental Spa + Med Spa）和 AI 全脸美学规划平台
- **政策制定者**：需建立牙科与医美跨学科操作的监管标准和培训体系
